newsitem.title: VIETNAM: New controversy for troubled Vietnam refinery plan.
newsitem.headline: New controversy for troubled Vietnam refinery plan.

text.p: Vietnam's troubled plan to build an oil refinery in the centre of the country ran into fresh controversy on Tuesday when it emerged there was an alternative plan for two smaller plants elsewhere.

State oil and gas firm Petrovietnam insisted the refinery, Vietnam's first, would still be built at Dung Quat, an undeveloped area of central Vietnam which is 1,000 km (600 miles) north of the country's oilfields and Ho Chi Minh City, the major consumer base.

"Dung Quat is fixed for the first refinery. The first refinery should be at Dung Quat. That's fixed and firm," Petrovietnam General Manager Do Van Ha told reporters in this southern city on the sidelines of an energy industry conference.

But a Ministry of Planning and Investment (MPI) official said there was an alternative proposal to build one refinery at either end of the country whose combined capacity would be equal to the planned 6.5 million tonnes per year of Dung Quat.

"Some people have...proposed not to build a 6.5-million-tonne refinery in central Vietnam, but a smaller one in the south and a second in the north," said Tran Quan Ngoc, the MPI's general director in charge of foreign investment in southern Vietnam.
"In our country there are different opinions on this," he said. "And some scientists and economy experts are selling this idea to the government. I think our government will consider it."
Delegates to the gathering, which was closed to foreign journalists, said there had been heated debate between officials on the location of the refinery at the conference.
The $1.3 billion refinery, which Vietnam says it desperately needs by early next century to cut a growing bill for petroleum product imports, has long been a subject of controversy.
A consortium of foreign firms which had planned to build the plant with Vietnam broke up recently after Petrovietnam rejected their demand for greater commercial and financial incentives.
The consortium had been put together to replace France's Total, which walked away from the project in 1995 after deciding the location made it "economically unviable".
Until now, there had been no sign from officials that the government was ready to consider other locations.
Prime Minister Vo Van Kiet is said to have backed Dung Quat to fight a "dumbell effect" of strong economic growth in the north and south and lagging development and poverty in the central region.
Ngoc said he would like to see a refinery in the south, which accounts for 65 percent of national petroleum product consumption, and said he hoped the government would change its mind.
"If our government accepts the proposal I think that foreign partners will get involved," he said.
He said it was far less likely that foreign partners would now join in the Dung Quat project, which Petrovietnam has said it is ready to build on its own.

However, Petrovietnam's Ha told Reuters the door would be left open for foreign investors to join the Dung Quat refinery at a later stage and noted continued interest from South Korea's LG Group and Malaysia's state oil firm Petronas.
"We are ready to talk as long as they accept our conditions," Ha said. "But we cannot wait, we cannot waste time, we need to go ahead. We'll start the bus, but leave the door open at the back."
